items.title: 829 Acres, 20 Years, and a Notice That Named No Tenant
items.summary: Four parcels to scale and the notice's dates, the rent by year, the affiliate's coal plan and the 6-1 vote.
items.content_html:
On January 30th the University of Alaska put 829 acres at Port MacKenzie up for lease on a notice that named no tenant.

829 acres. 20 years.

The notice named no tenant.

Terra Energy is the tenant.

Signed in late May for 20 years. The lease describes the Terra Energy Center Campus as "a large-scale industrial park," with energy generation, transmission, storage and distribution among its uses, and lets Terra sublease to future tenants.

An inholding in the borough's port.

The four parcels sit inside the Mat-Su Borough's 8,000-acre port district. Borough officials weren't told before the university signed. Port manager Dave Griffin said it "blows my mind."

Comment was asked on a notice that named no lessee and no use.

Posted January 30th. Comments closed at 5 p.m. on March 2nd. The lease was signed in late May, per university officials.

University land skips the best interest finding.

Projects on university land are exempt from the finding the state requires for major actions on state land, per the Mat-Su Sentinel.

$20,000 the first year. $586,000 once it operates.

Then $60,000 a year in years two and three. Construction would begin in 2029, and the report gives no figure for that year. Operations are targeted for 2030, and rent would rise 2 percent a year to the end of the 20-year lease.

The campus is part of a coal plan.

Flatlands Energy plans a coal plant near Skwentna. DOE selected the project for $89 million in engineering funding for a planned 1,250 MW plant and lists data centers among the loads it would serve. The university's own information doesn't highlight data centers.

The borough markets land with Terra.

In March the Assembly overrode a veto 6-1 to court large power users with Terra, data centers among them. Officials expect Terra to seek about 1,000 borough acres near the port.

Should a university land notice name its purpose before comments close?

items.title: Alaska's Second Wire Has a Passenger List
items.summary: Today's intertie, the new wire's stops and money, three bases and Murkowski's sentence, then five records, two saying data center.
items.content_html:
Alaska's planned second power line would end at Healy, south of Clear and Eielson, where the Air Force offered land for AI data centers.

Alaska's second wire has a passenger list.

Data centers aren't on it.

The money names the military, and mining.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright tied the project to "the major U.S. military expansion currently underway in Alaska" and to mining. DOE says the line adds a pathway to "major military installations." The release never says data center.

One line joins the two halves today.

AEA's Alaska Intertie runs 170 miles from Willow to Healy. The state built it in the mid-1980s.

The record names its stops and its price. Not its route.

The Alaska delegation lists the Beluga substation, West Susitna, Willow and Healy. AEA's Curtis Thayer told the Alaska Beacon the federal money will likely go to engineering, planning and permitting.

On Railbelt bases, land offered for AI data centers.

Proposals were due June 29th. None had been awarded as of late September, per the American Homefront Project. Most of Alaska's bases use power that flows through the intertie, the Alaska Beacon reports.

One corridor. No second path between the halves.

"I am not a proponent of data centers down at JBER or at our interior installations because we are not able to support them because of an insecure energy base at this time."

Five records. Two say "data center." The one with the money doesn't.

Reading them side by side is this deck's work, not DOE's.

Should the Beluga to Healy line be planned with data center load in it, or without?

items.title: Of 150 Cited, 119 Used AI. The Rule Says Devices.
items.summary: A drawn hall of 10,500 seats shows 150 cited and 119 for AI. Then come the clause, two years of reports kept apart and the November calendar.
items.content_html:
AI cases are now most of UAA's conduct caseload by its own report. The rule behind them says "devices" and never names AI.

Of 150 cited, 119 used AI.

The rule says "devices."

1.1 percent.

119 of the more than 10,500 students at UAA last semester. Small as a share, AI cases are now the majority of the conduct office's caseload, the report says.

That clause of UAA's student conduct code is how AI cases are handled. It never names AI. Each instructor decides what is authorized, course by course.

Every syllabus must address AI. No two have to agree.

Professors may allow as much or as little AI as they like, a structure UAA's Faculty Senate asked for. UAA discourages AI checkers. Many faculty use them anyway, writing professor Andrew Harnish said.

Two reports. Two different counts.

The draft says a human decides.

Under today's clause, that human is each instructor.

Should the regents write what a student may do with AI, or leave it to each syllabus?

Student government member Brigitta Taaga pushed back that the draft didn't go far enough.

items.title: More Than Three Alaskas of Power, Planned for Prudhoe Bay
items.summary: What EIA measures is drawn sharp, all 152 plants mapped to scale. The reported money sits in fog. The terms are a closed pipe blind.
items.content_html:
3,000 megawatts. Phase one of a gas plant planned near Prudhoe Bay for AI data centers nearly equals all 152 power plants in Alaska.

More than three Alaskas of power, planned for Prudhoe Bay.

Each lit bore is 100 MW.

Phase one is about the size of every power plant in Alaska combined. The full plan is more than three times it.

A borough's plant, for AI data centers.

The North Slope Borough and Twenty First Century Utilities (TFC) are developing North Slope Power to feed colocated AI data centers. The borough's own utility runs seven village plants, 21.4 MW in all.

The gas is already here.

Two outlets, two areas, two counts. Gas is already Alaska's main fuel for electricity, per EIA. In March the borough's mayor and TFC took the plan to CERAWeek in Texas.

TFC's proposal listed climate change among 10 North Slope challenges. Where it said how it would tackle each one, climate change got "N/A."

$6.2 million in.

A $1.2 million no-bid feasibility contract in November 2025. Another $5 million of public funds in March. Both as reported by the Alaska Current.

The terms aren't public.

That is the resolution behind the $5 million, as the Alaska Current quotes it. It says the Borough would "initially" keep that majority. The financial structure is not public.

Before the next public dollar, should the borough publish the terms?

items.title: Ten Minutes of Every Hour, The Count an AI Drone Must Beat
items.summary: The Togiak's 119,298 sockeye are traced from a ten-minute window to their own error bar.
items.content_html:
"The results have exceeded my expectations," Norm Van Vactor said in July of his Wood River AI drone pilot.

Togiak missed by 702 fish. Its tower counted 10 minutes an hour.

Ten minutes, times six.

Bristol Bay's towers count each bank for 10 minutes of every hour, then expand. Crews work around the clock with hand clickers. At six to one, the Togiak's 119,298 rests on roughly 19,883 fish someone saw.

The error bar runs three times the miss.

ADF&G put the average sampling CV across nine Bristol Bay tower projects at 0.02 in 2004 and 2005. On the Togiak's 119,298 that is about 2,400 fish either way. It assumes no miscounts inside the ten minutes.

The rule was tested on 12 to 80 hours.

In 1965 and 1966, crews counted whole hours and compared them with the first 10 minutes, expanded. Errors ran generally under 10 percent, with no significant bias.

Eight towers counted 12.3 million of 15.6 million.

A box opens. A drone takes off.

A computer vision model is learning to pick out the salmon in its footage.

A key press for every fish.

Technicians press a key each time a fish crosses a line drawn on the footage. The first phase logged 256 flights and 17,552 images, stitched into 117 orthomosaics. The project lead says it spots fish 12 to 18 hours before the tower.

Matching the tower can't be the bar.

The pilot plans to test its model against Fish and Game tower counts next. Tower sampling error averaged about 2 percent in 2004 and 2005. The team's goal is a count with a stated confidence. Write the margin first.

Before the Wood River test runs, who should set the passing margin?

items.title: Alaska's SNAP Bill Reads a Year That Opened Thursday
items.summary: Steel instruments read the law's shares and Alaska's record, then the state's system, staffing and 2028 fix.
items.content_html:
Alaska's SNAP payment error rate ran 57, 60.4, 24.7 and 23 percent from 2022 to 2025.

Alaska's SNAP bill reads a year that opened Thursday.

Fiscal 2027 is read either way.

From fiscal 2029, a state's share uses its error rate from three fiscal years before. Fiscal 2030 reads fiscal 2027, opened October 1st, whichever start applies.

The first share moved on Thursday.

Washington's share of SNAP administration fell from 50 to 25 percent, so Alaska now pays 75. Legislative Finance estimates about $6.6 million more a year. The Anchorage Daily News reported nearly $11 million.

The second share is a staircase.

Under 6 percent, a state pays none of the benefit cost. At 10 or more, it pays 15 percent.

The record, against the statute's lines.

Alaska's 2025 rate, times 1.5, cleared 20 percent, which moved its start to fiscal 2029. Clear it again in 2026 and the start moves to 2030.

"COBOL on a mainframe."

How the state describes EIS, its legacy eligibility system. ARIES, the newer one, holds only MAGI Medicaid.

218 of 332 positions filled.

The yearly average left 34.3 percent vacant. "During periods when Alaska had significant workload backlogs, that had a larger impact on the state's error rate," the Department of Health wrote.

The fix is scheduled for 2028.

Milestone 2, estimated at $20 million, began in October 2025. Milestone 2.5, estimated at $5 million, would move SNAP data off the mainframe. The Department says the biggest gains wait for full modernization.

Save this for the day fiscal 2026's rate is published.

items.title: Three Yeas, Three Short, No Start Date
items.summary: Gold marks Alaska's three yeas in a 100-cup Senate tray at 57 and a 432-cup House tray at 417, beside two unturned sand-glasses, a three-bay exemption cabinet, SB 250's 14 and 5 and a steel rule with no enactment tick.
items.content_html:
On the Alaska Senate floor in Juneau on May 16th, data center bill SB 250 passed 14 to 5.

Alaska's three votes were yes. The Senate fell three short.

Cloture needed 60. It got 57.

Three-fifths of the Senate had to agree just to take it up. The motion was then withdrawn. Lisa Murkowski and Dan Sullivan both voted yea. The House had passed it two weeks before.

Two weeks earlier, the House passed it 417 to 3.

Nick Begich voted yea. Republicans went 210 to 0, Democrats 206 to 3 and the one independent voted yea. Suspending the rules took two-thirds.

A standard for computing sites of 100 MW and up.

Rates would be designed to recover that cost from the customer, even if it ends its contract. Each state regulator would have to consider the standard and decide.

Both clocks start on a day that hasn't happened.

It also counts backward.

A state skips both clocks if, before enactment, it had put a comparable standard in place, held a proceeding on one, or its legislature had voted on one. Has Alaska done any of the three?

Alaska's Senate passed SB 250, 14 to 5. A House panel held it.

It passed May 16th and was heard and held in House Community and Regional Affairs two days later. Does one chamber's vote count as "the State legislature has voted"?

Every date on the record, and the one not set.

Three yeas. Three short. No start date.

Save this. If the date is ever set, both clocks run from it.

A state skips both clocks if, before enactment, it had put a comparable standard in place, held a proceeding on one, or its legislature had voted on one. Has Alaska done any of the three?

Alaska's Senate passed SB 250, 14 to 5. A House panel held it.

Every date on the record, and the one not set.

Three yeas. Three short. No start date.

items.title: Right for Most of Alaska. Wrong for Kodiak.
items.summary: From Shelikof Strait the camera drops to Bull Lake and the trooper's AI search, pulls back to five bird zones, then sinks to the mud where the $150 lands.
items.content_html:
A Kodiak court file holds an AI answer's September 1st, the law's October 8th and a September 5th snipe hunt.

Right for most of Alaska. Wrong for Kodiak.

On September 5th, a Kodiak hunter took three snipe.

She had searched "Snipe season" on her phone. She told a trooper that, according to Google, the season began September 1st. Kodiak's zone opens October 8th.

The zone was in the parentheses.

"ADF&G sets the Wilson's Snipe hunting season in Alaska generally from September 1st through December 16th (or matching general migratory bird/waterfowl windows depending on the specific zone...)"

Five zones. Two opening days.

Southeast, Gulf Coast and Northern open September 1st. Kodiak and the Pribilof and Aleutian zone open October 8th. Unimak Island goes with the Gulf Coast.

Same length. Only the start moves.

She called troopers on herself the same afternoon.

No contest. A $150 fine.

The charge was a Class A misdemeanor. She pleaded no contest and was fined $150, the Alaska Beacon reported.

"I expect we'll see more of this type of thing in the future."

Spokesman Austin McDaniel says it's the first time he thinks the department has seen AI cited, and it doesn't track these cases. Google's own help page says AI Overviews "can and will make mistakes."

Read the zone before the date.

DPS says the one source of truth for hunts is ADF&G's regulations and emergency orders.

Alaska has about 0.2 percent of the country's people and about 7.3 percent of its funded E-Rate commitments.

Alaska holds 7.3 percent of E-Rate.

items.title: A Say on 5 Megawatts at Eielson, Until September 30th
items.summary: A wetland map and five spots offered to developers. Reactor, coal plant and data center sized in 5 megawatt blocks. Murkowski and two utilities on power, then the comment address.
items.content_html:
You have until September 30th to comment on site work for a 5 megawatt microreactor near wetlands at Eielson Air Force Base.

The public gets a say on 5 megawatts at Eielson.

A reactor site, east of the runway's south end.

The Air Force wants public input on work at the preferred site for a 5 megawatt Oklo microreactor, near Spruce Lake. It sits near wetlands, so federal law requires the ask first.

Clear it, dig it, fill it, level it.

That is the preconstruction work Air Force officials describe. Their wetland delineation for a draft Environmental Assessment finished in July. KUAC reports the draft is expected late next year.

Oklo would own it. The Air Force would buy the power.

It would supply the base electricity and heat. A 30-year fixed-price contract could follow a Nuclear Regulatory Commission license. Officials hope for 2030, if only an assessment is needed.

Same base. A second process.

Five spots near Eielson, offered to developers.

The Air Force solicitation covered land at JBER, Eielson and Clear, about 4,700 acres in all. Proposals were due June 29th. KUAC reported no project awarded as of mid-September.

5 megawatts, against a 100 megawatt bar.

Separate processes, shown for scale. Nothing in the record says the reactor would serve a data center.

"we are not able to support them because of an insecure energy base at this time"

Chugach Electric and Golden Valley Electric told ADN in May that they can't produce enough electricity for large data centers as Cook Inlet gas dwindles.

Comment by September 30th.

items.title: A Bigger Tank, Not a Bigger Engine. Bradley Lake and 2030
items.summary: On a relief map and a cutaway, a proposed 4.6-mile tunnel carries Dixon Glacier water to Bradley Lake for more energy, not more megawatts, ending on a 1991 to 2032 calendar that splits what exists from what is only filed.
items.content_html:
Fairbanks is burning 250,000 gallons of diesel a day, AEA's Curtis Thayer says.

About 38 percent more electricity. Its dam is slated for 2030.

A bigger tank, not a bigger engine.

A new diversion dam would send Dixon Glacier meltwater through a 4.6-mile tunnel into Bradley Lake and raise its pool about 16 feet. Capacity barely moves. The plant gets more water to spend.

4.6 miles of tunnel to carry glacier water.

AEA estimates the cost at about $400 million and expects construction to start in 2027 if federal approvals come through. FERC has the application under project P-8221-124.

It buys energy, not megawatts.

Today, Dixon's meltwater runs down the Martin River.

"There's nothing for tomorrow. There's nothing for next year."

Natural gas fuels about 80 percent of Southcentral's power generation, per KTUU. Fairbanks is burning 250,000 gallons of diesel a day, Thayer said. "They never did that last year."

The AI pitch runs on the same calendar.

The Air Force offered twelve parcels, about 4,700 acres, at JBER, Clear and Eielson for AI data centers. Its solicitation said the JBER sites had insufficient power and needed a new Chugach connection.

What exists, and what is only filed.

Until the glacier water arrives, should Railbelt AI data centers bring their own power?

items.title: Who Read It? The Labels on 90 Alaska News Articles
items.summary: A counter of 1,258 recorded meetings is set against one Axon police-data story that ran with no editor review on record.
items.content_html:
Alaska News says its old footer told every reader an article was "reviewed by editors," whether or not it was.

"Source access is not the same thing as editorial judgment."

90 articles in 48 hours. One human name on the review line.

Alaska News says every article carries a line saying whether a person reviewed it. Every human name on those lines was the editor-in-chief's, Cale Green.

The machine already does the reading.

Alaska News says its tool has sat through 1,258 recorded public meetings and 3,092 hours of audio. A team of five based in Anchorage runs it. How would a reader know who read each draft?

The right invention is the label.

When an editor has read the whole piece, the article says reviewed by, with a name. When no one has, it says that instead. Its old footer told every reader "reviewed by editors," regardless.

What the labels on 90 articles said.

Counted from the alaskanews.com news sitemap, September 26th. A label describes process, not accuracy, and can change after a later review.

Plenty of reading. One name on the record.

The risk it names itself.

Alaska News says some articles publish without a person reading them first. Its story on the Anchorage Assembly's Axon police-data memo ran as "AI-assisted. No editor review is on record for this article." That doesn't make it wrong. It tells you to check.

"The strongest protection is not my assurance. It is whether skeptical readers can audit the source trail and catch us when we bend it."

Alaska News says the source wins when a summary and its record disagree. Readers can only audit what the label tells them.

Should every AI-drafted story in Alaska say who reviewed it, by name?

items.title: Six Data Center Sites. Two Answer to Juneau.
items.summary: The maps ink the two state sites in gold and ring the four federal ones in dashes. All four candidates are quoted at equal size.
items.content_html:
From the North Slope to Cook Inlet, six sites could host data centers, and Alaska's next governor could reach two.

A disclosure. This deck was produced by an automated studio running on Claude, a model made by Anthropic. The Alaska Beacon reports that Kreiss-Tomkins' campaign has received large donations from people employed by Anthropic. The deck leaves that report out and quotes all four candidates at equal size, in alphabetical order, so no candidate is framed by it.

Six sites in play for data centers. Two answer to Juneau.

Two sit on state land. Four are federal calls.

The North Slope lease and the Houston land are decided in the Department of Natural Resources, whose commissioner the governor appointed. The Air Force decides three bases. FERC decides Cook Inlet's preliminary permit.

What they say about data centers.

"I'm a big believer in data centers." He said the groups he is talking to would produce their own power (Bronson, Republican, Commonwealth North forum). "I support a moratorium on data center development in Alaska until the Legislature can pass a comprehensive regulatory framework for that development in Alaska." (Kreiss-Tomkins, Democrat, September 8th forum). "I think we need to embrace it." Any data center, he said, must "bring their own energy." (Taylor, Republican, September 8th forum). "I will never allow Alaska to be littered with hyperscale data centers that take our resources and spoil our lands." (Wilson, Republican, by text message). Order is alphabetical by surname, not a ranking. Quotes as reported by the Alaska Beacon.

Milepost 390. State land, 50 years.

DNR proposes a 50-year lease on 715.4 acres beside the Dalton Highway, 26 miles south of Deadhorse. Its final decision would be signed by the Division of Oil and Gas, under authority delegated from the DNR commissioner. The same decision says what powers it.

"not interconnected to the Railbelt or any other Alaska utility grid"

A gas plant designed for 1 to 3 GW, all used on site. Two candidates raised the same point.

One state decision, three federal ones.

DNR proposes giving AIDEA about 19,950 acres two miles north of Houston. No final decision appears on the notice. The Air Force offered to lease about 4,700 acres at JBER, Eielson and Clear, with no award yet.

Filings close the day before the vote.

DeepGreen proposes a 100 MW subsea data center in Cook Inlet, and FERC decides its preliminary permit. The Kenai Peninsula Borough filed to intervene. The deadline is November 2nd.

Who signs each one.

Preliminary decision. No final decision on the notice, for the North Slope lease (ADL 422741), which DNR signs under the commissioner's delegation. For a data center bill, the Legislature, then the governor. Senate passed it 14 to 5, per the Beacon. The House didn't. A veto takes two-thirds to override. For JBER, Eielson and Clear, the Department of the Air Force. Proposals closed June 29th. No award. For the Houston land to AIDEA, DNR. No final decision on the notice. For Cook Inlet (P-15423-000), FERC, on a preliminary permit. Filings close November 2nd.

Save this. Check it again after November 3rd.

In June, controlled fires were set along the Nenana-Totchaket Road, and machines from Nenana's airport had 8 hours to find them alone.

items.title: What Mat-Su's Plate Reader Ban Actually Reaches
items.summary: The ordinance and its information memorandum carry six of the nine frames. The borough's own law enforcement page carries two. The Anchorage Daily News carries one.
items.content_html:
Five agencies police the Matanuska-Susitna Borough. The borough is not one of them.

Mat-Su banned plate readers the night it was heard.

ADOPTED UNANIMOUSLY. IN FORCE ON ADOPTION.

The borough wrote down what the machine is.

The chapter defines it as one or more high-speed camera units, alone or combined with algorithms and optical character recognition, turning images of plates, makes, models, colors and unique vehicle identifiers into computer-readable data.

The subject never changes.

No Borough department, division, employee, or agent

It can't collect the data. It can't be handed it.

"The Borough and its departments are prohibited from accessing, querying, uploading data to, or receiving data from any ALPR operator, network, database, or private surveillance network."

"The borough does not have police powers."

That is the borough's own sentence, on its own site. Some of its cities do have them. The state troopers patrol here.

Five agencies police this boundary.

ABOUT 117,400 PEOPLE LIVE INSIDE THIS LINE, PER STATE LABOR ESTIMATES FOR 2025

The operator it names is the borough itself.

An ALPR Operator, in the chapter's own words, is any Borough department, division, employee, or third-party contractor acting under contract with the Borough. Eight borough officials signed the routing block between August 19th and August 21st, weeks before it reached the floor. On September 15th, another assembly took up the same question.

One body wrote the limit. The other kept drafting.

Anchorage Assembly members voted unanimously to postpone their own police surveillance ordinance, AO 2026-108(S), to their regular meeting on October 20th, the Anchorage Daily News reported. The paper quoted one member asking for stronger language and stronger protections.

A limit written before the power exists.

Mat-Su bound its own departments, its own money and its own contracts, unanimously, for a machine it has no police powers to run.

items.title: Priority, Not Permission
items.summary: The record is one federal notice with three blanks in it, and one September 14th newspaper report quoting Curtis W. Thayer for the state.
items.content_html:
66 data center pods. 330 to 350 turbines. 3.5 miles of cable. The federal notice never says how much seabed.

So far, the Cook Inlet data center is a document.

Applied.

DeepGreen Cook Inlet SPV, LLC filed an application for a preliminary permit on February 11th and supplemented it on June 26th. FERC signed the notice September 1st. The Federal Register published it September 4th.

Proposed.

66 modular subsea-compute hives, which the notice also calls data center pods. 330 to 350 marine hydrokinetic turbines. A 3.5 mile, 115 kV hybrid power and fiber-optic armored cable, landing in the Nikiski Industrial Corridor.

Priority.

"The sole purpose of a preliminary permit, if issued, is to grant the permit holder priority to file a license application during the permit term." It would not authorize construction, land-disturbing work or entry onto property owned by others.

100 megawatts

"The estimated annual generation of the DeepGreen Project would be 100 megawatts, which would primarily be utilized to power the subsea data center." A megawatt measures power, not a year of it. That is the notice's own wording.

What it says. What it doesn't.

IN THE FEDERAL NOTICE

Nobody called.

"We're going to file to intervene and oppose it, just so we have a position. We've had no communication with them." The Peninsula Clarion reports that DeepGreen cited AEA's own planned Cook Inlet PowerLink, 38 miles and up to 200 megawatts, in its federal filing. ORPC says it has no affiliation with the project and is not participating in it.

Anyone. Including a rival.

The window takes comments, protests and motions to intervene. It also takes competing applications for the same site, and notices of intent to file one, under 18 CFR 4.36. A place in line is a thing other people can want.

File. November 2nd.

Comments, protests, motions to intervene and competing applications are due 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time on November 2nd, on FERC docket P-15423-000, through the Commission's eFiling system. The Peninsula Clarion reports the deadline moved from October 31st, a Saturday.

items.title: Every Notice Went Up
items.summary: The ten items as the ordinance writes them, what the state found, and the blank in the form.
items.content_html:
Who has to be told before somebody changes the weather over the southern Kenai? The answer is not the borough underneath.

EVERY NOTICE WENT UP. NONE CAME DOWN.

19 FLARES OVER THE SOUTHERN KENAI, AUGUST 23RD

Notice was given. It went up.

Federal law bars anyone from changing the weather without filing a report, and the rule sets that filing at least 10 days before the activity begins. Rainmaker asked Alaska DNR first, and it answered with a letter of no objection.

The drones flew over state land.

Because the flight was over state and not borough land, no borough permission was needed. The borough's own attorney put the limit in writing, that a second class borough has no authority to fully regulate this or the airspace.

19 million gallons is a hundredth of an inch.

Rainmaker flew 10 drone flights on August 23rd and its report puts the result at about 57 acre-feet, or roughly 19 million gallons, which works out to about 0.01 inches across the area. The state calls these modeled estimates, not water measured at the ground.

The borough's port was never drilled.

Rainmaker's press release was the first notice the borough had that drones carrying weather modification payloads were operating inside it. The flight was over state land, so no borough permission was needed.

The borough wrote a form.

Ten required items, on borough land only.

Ten questions. None about the model.

The state's own letter says the company uses drones, atmospheric observations, weather radar and modeling to identify clouds and conditions suitable for seeding. Every one of the ten items asks about the payload, the pyrotechnics or the flight.

Everyone can ask. Almost nobody can act.

Alaska has no framework specific to weather modification and no state permit is required for cloud seeding. This session carries 856 bills and not one of them is on the subject. Federal law takes a filing, not a permission.

One room. October 20th.

The public hearing on the ordinance is October 20th, and if the Assembly enacts it, it takes effect immediately. Until then it is introduced and not law.

items.title: Utqiagvik Observers and an Arctic Ocean Model
items.summary: The deck holds a season disc broken open where the records disagree, the observer's October 1st, 2019 entry, and ten author slots.
items.content_html:
Validation is what science does to data to decide if it is good enough. A paper published September 18th inverts that.

"Everyone is waiting for snow."

The model had already frozen the sea.

In 2019 the model froze the sea early. The coast froze late.

The paper publishes the direction and no magnitude. This drawing does the same. The two marks sit inside a declared break, so the space between them carries no value.

"It has rained so much that the roads are falling apart and we may have broken a temperature record. Everyone is waiting for snow. The bowhead whales are not close to Barrow yet either."

Over 12,000 observations, more than 1,500 km of coast.

Observers document sea ice, ocean conditions, weather, fish and marine wildlife, and unusual or extreme events. The program and the one before it have run since 2006.

which made hunting especially difficult.

Observers reported late freeze-up, warm conditions and stormy weather

The fall hunt took one whale.

Historical fall harvests have reached up to about 30. Spring is a separate season and is not in this count.

Most of the time the two records agree.

The paper reports the model generally captured the timing of seasonal changes, especially the end of the open water season. That is what makes one wrong season worth finding.

Ten authors. The observers are among them.

The paper says Indigenous observers are co-authors and shape its research questions, the interpretation of results and the priorities for model development. It argues Indigenous Knowledge can identify model deficiencies that conventional metrics miss.

A model can be broadly right and still wrong about the season you live in.

items.title: Out of Nenana and Back, With the Finding Pending
items.summary: The deck holds the paired samples, the hangar laboratory at the same airport, and five logged channels as empty rows.
items.content_html:
A 1,000 kilometre blood flight out of Nenana is documented down to five logged sensor channels. The finding is not published.

1,000 km of blood. Out of Nenana. Back to Nenana.

8 h 47 min aloft. Back at Nenana.

ACUASI, part of the University of Alaska Fairbanks, flew human blood for the International Testing Agency. UAF puts the flight at 8 hours and 47 minutes. The ITA's own release says only several hours.

Two samples each. One flew. One stayed.

The Interior Region EMS Council drew the blood at UAF the day before. It was anonymised and chilled, then split into two groups.

A 31 foot span, and a 200 pound bay.

They are twin engine aircraft with three cargo drop doors, and they work off dirt, grass, ice or tarmac. UAF is one of nine FAA designated test sites for uncrewed aircraft.

A circle tests the cargo. A line delivers the care.

The flight began and ended at Nenana Municipal Airport. Closing a route holds everything still except the blood, which is how you find out whether the blood minds. It also means this test measured a sample and not a delivery.

The distance was the point. Alaska had the distance.

"I'm not saying we're ready today, but I think we'll be ready tomorrow."

The laboratory was in a building at the same airport.

Sysmex equipped a satellite laboratory inside an airport hangar with XN-Series analysers. Dr. Sven Voss, who directs the WADA accredited laboratory in Dresden, ran it. Both groups were analysed on site.

Alaska supplied the distance.

Cathy Cahill, who directs ACUASI, describes nurses taking samples in a community and getting the medication back before they leave. That is a line, not a loop.

items.summary: Both award rows are drawn as freight on one aircraft floor, with the ten rows out of 217 that name a machine.
items.content_html:
Alaska's rural health program awarded $250,000 for a drone plan on August 14th. On September 4th it awarded $4,171,115 for aircraft.

THE AWARD SAYS IMPLEMENTATION NOT PLANNING

Ryan Air was awarded $4,171,115 to deploy "autonomous cargo drones and electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft" carrying pharmaceuticals and moving patients across roadless communities. IA means aircraft, not a study.

A FAMILY FREIGHT LINE WITH A GRANT

Ryan Air started in 1953 in the village of Unalakleet and is managed by the third generation of the Ryan family. It serves 80 villages throughout Western Alaska and operates 24 aircraft out of eight hubs.

AIRCRAFT TAKE THE PLACE OF AMBULANCES

402 Alaskan communities depend on aviation for year round access, where aircraft often take the place of cars, school buses, semitrucks, and ambulances. That is 82 percent of the state's communities, served by 235 airports. Ryan Air's own proposal calls the gap "life-threatening".

ONE PROGRAM. TWO LOADS.

THE INTERIOR GOT A YEAR TO PLAN

Tanana Chiefs Conference took $250,000 for a planning year on the same idea, a drone pharmaceutical route from a Fairbanks hub to 42 Interior villages across 94,000 square miles. Tanana Chiefs says winter medication delays of 5 to 14 days are common.

FIRST THE WAIVER THEN THE AIRCRAFT

Tanana Chiefs names the University of Alaska Fairbanks Alaska Center for Unmanned Aircraft Systems Integration as its partner on FAA beyond visual line of sight waivers. ACUASI was selected as one of the first seven FAA unmanned aircraft test sites.

TEN ROWS NAME A MACHINE

THE ROUNDS ARE NOT FINISHED

Roughly $65 million is still expected to be awarded ahead of a federal deadline of October 30th. The next Friday is the next row.

items.title: The Permit Knows Where the Machine Is
items.summary: Two numbers and one blank sit in the stock table of the Arctic permit NMFS issued the Navy on September 10th.
items.content_html:
Two numbers and one blank sit in the stock table of the Arctic permit NMFS issued the Navy on September 10th.

The permit can find the robot. It can't count the seal.

Sound is how the machine knows where it is.

Above the ice, a glider gets its position from a satellite modem. Under the ice, that signal can't reach it. The notice says gliders then navigate by trilateration from moored acoustic sound sources, the geometry of intersecting circles.

30 seconds, every four hours, all year.

Up to six moorings are fixed acoustic navigation sources at 900 to 950 Hz. Each sends a 30 second pulse every four hours. Two buoys drift on that cycle. Levels this year stay under 185 dB re 1 uPa at 1 m.

About 639,237 square kilometres of water.

Its closest point to the Alaska coast is 204 kilometres, or 110 nautical miles. The work crosses the US exclusive economic zone, the high seas north of Alaska, and part of Canada's.

Every zone here, drawn at one scale.

Vessels hold 457 metres from observed cetaceans and 183 metres from other observed marine mammals. Deployment and recovery of a source carries a 55 metre zone. The estimated range to temporary hearing threshold shift is under 15 metres.

A 22 day cruise. A full year of transmission.

The cruise is planned for 22 days from September 22nd, on a ship the notice calls ice strengthened rather than icebreaking. The sources keep transmitting until September 13th, 2027. Mitigation that needs an observer works only while one is aboard.

The same page gives the seal's number as UND.

Beaufort beluga, 39,258, from a 1992 survey. Eastern Chukchi beluga, 13,305, from 2017, at a coefficient of variation of 0.51. Arctic ringed seal, the one species here listed as threatened, undetermined.

Position, fixed. The rest is undetermined.

The authorization runs from September 14th and by statute can't run longer than a year. This is the ninth year of the project. It relies on a Biological Opinion issued on September 13th, 2022. Three private citizens wrote in.

The robot's fix or the seal's number.

Year 10 is already inside the comment scope of Year 9. Which of those two numbers should the next authorization improve?

items.title: One Agenda. Two Items. One Vote.
items.summary: The carousel plots the network's real size on a log rule. 11 cameras integrated against 238 registered as of August 27th, 2026, under a 750 ceiling.
items.content_html:
A hearing on Anchorage's police AI rule was set for September 1st, 2026. The camera money passed 8 to 4 that night. The rule got no vote.

UPDATE. $598,998 passed 8 to 4. The rule got no vote.

Three of the four no votes wrote the rule.

Keith McCormick, Daniel Volland and Sydney Scout proposed AO 2026-108. All three voted against the money. They lost 8 to 4 on the night of September 1st, 2026.

What the money is, and what it is not.

The $598,998 comes from federal asset forfeitures, per a memorandum submitted to the Assembly. Chief Sean Case says it moves the crime center to its final location. The Assembly approved $11.8 million last year for the underlying system. ADN reported the Assembly considered a $600,000 ThunderCat contract.

750 is the ceiling, not the count.

The gap from 11 to 238 is wider than the gap from 238 to 750. Registered means APD knows the camera exists. Integrated means APD can pull the feed, through a CORE device from Axon.

Three gates. None of them struck.

ADN reports the ordinance would require Assembly permission before AI with human feature recognition is added to the network. Alaska Public Media reports it would require a warrant before data goes to federal agencies. ADN reports the technology would face a period of temporary approval and annual reporting.

CODE.

"Let's put this into code now, so that when power changes, when the political winds shift, as they always do, we have protections for the people, no matter who is overseeing and implementing the system."

What is already in code. And what is only practice.

Municipal use of facial recognition technology was officially banned by the Anchorage Assembly in 2023, per APD's own page. All scanned license plate data is automatically deleted after 14 days. Traffic camera footage is overwritten every 3 to 5 days. The camera registry is voluntary, the owner keeps control at all times, and APD must obtain permission to access video. APD does not use Flock cameras.

Fourteen days, read twice.

How long a scanned plate lives. Deleted after 14 days, per APD's own page. How long the rule waited. September 1st, 2026 to September 15th, 2026.

The rule is expected back on September 15th, 2026.

Sponsors plan to bring AO 2026-108 back to the Assembly. Public testimony is how a resident gets read into the record.

items.title: Run Both Instruments, or Lose the Record
items.summary: Slide 06 draws the survey gear's seabed footprint at true area, and slide 08 sets the three pools on one rail where the third bracket is empty.
items.content_html:
When a machine takes a ship's place on a fish survey, how do you tell a change in the fish from a change in the instrument?

Two instruments on the same line, in parallel. That's the bill.

The new instrument is allowed to be different.

"Consistency in information that FIS data products provide is more important than consistency in FIS methods."

Agreement is bought. It is never assumed.

The framework calls for "incremental incorporation and calibration of new technologies" rather than "a wholesale replacement of existing methods that would disrupt the historical baseline of a time series" (C05). The most common way to do it is to run the old method and the new one in parallel for a fixed period (C07).

Ground the net can't cross.

The camera can see it. It can't hold it.

NOAA says the camera techniques "are not intended to replace hands-on sampling because physical specimens are essential for critical data, including age, feeding habits, and body condition" (C20). A near-infrared machine reads an otolith in 30 to 50 seconds, more than 10 times faster than a human at a microscope (C18).

0.006%

The framework's own figure for the share of total Alaska seabed area that bottom trawl survey gear contacts, offered against calls to ban extractive sampling (C08).

The record is being pulled from two sides at once.

The framework lists funding, vessel availability, new sampling objectives and new technology as human forces that break a time series (C09). NOAA says fish populations have shifted into deeper water or farther north where surveys have not traditionally been conducted (C12).

Twelve days later, the same question, on a smaller boat.

On September 15th, 2026 the North Pacific Council's Partial Coverage Fishery Monitoring Advisory Committee reviews the draft 2027 Annual Deployment Plan (C22, C23). The 2026 plan defines a no selection pool, vessels with no probability of carrying an observer or an electronic monitoring system on any trip that season (C28).

The committee takes comment letters.

The draft 2027 Annual Deployment Plan had not yet been posted on the meeting page as of September 6th, 2026 (C25). The Federal Register notice says public comment letters will be accepted and should be submitted electronically through the meeting page (C24).

items.title: The Half That Lasts. Alaska's quiet land decision.
items.summary: The state's own words on use, the classification order beneath them and the comment count.
items.content_html:
The state held two public meetings on a proposed 19,950 acre transfer to AIDEA near Houston and took no testimony at either.

19,950 acres. Three state notices. None says data center.

The state's own words go this far and stop.

Three notices govern the conveyance. July 10th, August 19th and August 24th, 2026. The furthest any of them goes on use is "to create a multi-use industrial and energy development district". The July notice states no intended use at all.

One window is carrying two decisions.

About 19,950 acres would go to AIDEA under a noncompetitive public and charitable use conveyance, case. A Draft Land Classification Order,, rides the same window. The land is reported to transfer at no cost. Both close on the same date.

The ground was here before the file number.

Most of it changes what it is for.

About 15,100 acres now designated Forestry, Habitat and Water Resources would be reclassified as Settlement. A tenant can arrive or never arrive. A classification stays until somebody changes it back.

Three named uses, and one with nothing in it.

Forestry, Habitat and Water Resources are what this ground is classified for today. Settlement is what the order proposes. AIDEA's plan lists possibilities and not commitments, data centers among them. No tenant, job number, energy need or water use has been named.

More than 2,000 people have already written in.

Scoping opened July 10th, 2026 and the original close was August 19th. More than 2,000 written comments had arrived by August 24th, by the department's own count. Two informational meetings were held and neither took testimony. Houston's council voted unanimously against the process.

The acres are known. The place is not.

A survey township is 36 sections of one square mile. The conveyance is about 19,950 acres, which is 31.2 sections of the 72 in Township 18 North and Township 19 North. Where those acres sit has not been published.

Comment closes 5:00 p.m. Monday, September 14th, 2026.

items.title: Counted Twice. Fairbanks Votes on the Machines.
items.summary: The clerk's ballot title, the tolerance beside the measured gap, Haney's case in full and the five dates still open.
items.content_html:
"If the hand count is to check on the machines, then why do we have the machines?" Barbara Haney sponsored Fairbanks Proposition 3.

Counted by hand. Counted by machine. Same answer. Now Fairbanks votes.

Requiring all ballots to be hand counted and prohibiting electronic tabulation

Only registered borough voters would conduct the counts, and official results would come solely from manual hand counts. The petition was submitted with 2,706 signatures against a requirement of 2,391, and the clerk recertified it on August 5th, 2026.

3,338 ballots, checked by hand.

A 2025 ordinance created the audit and passed 5 to 4. A canvass board hand verified the votes on 3,338 ballots, two precincts out of 32 plus the early voting station.

The tolerance was 33 ballots wide. The gap was zero.

The 2025 ordinance defined failure in advance, a discrepancy greater than 1 percent between the hand count and the machine tabulation. On the sampled ballots the machines came back 100 percent accurate, so the trip point was never approached.

"If the hand count is to check on the machines, then why do we have the machines?"

Haney was one of four who voted against creating that audit, per KUAC. Tammie Wilson and Brett Rotermund were two of the other three.

Two of 32 precincts were sampled. Thirty were not, and were never claimed.

Two years. No estimate.

Hand counting would start with the 2027 cycle, so October 6th is still machine tabulated. If Proposition 3 passes, the ordinance is law for two years and neither the Assembly nor the voters can repeal, modify or negate it. The ordinance carries no fiscal analysis.

Register by September 6th.

A test can settle a measurement. It can't settle what a count is for.

What result would have changed your mind?

items.title: Eight Machines, One Sheet
items.summary: The eight awards with dollars. The four Friday rounds at true width. An empty ACTS ALONE column.
items.content_html:
AI in Alaska usually means data centers and gigawatts. In the state's rural health awards it means a note taker for about $25,500.

The robot is in Ketchikan. The stroke reader is everywhere.

TWELVE BOROUGHS CUT OUT OF ONE STATE SHEET

185 awards. Eight machines.

Announced on four Fridays since August 7th, across all 30 boroughs and census areas. Eight of them buy a machine that reads, decides or flies.

The biggest machine is a handle.

PeaceHealth Ketchikan Medical Center takes it for the first robotic assisted minimally invasive surgery in Southern Southeast, serving four boroughs across water. A surgeon drives it.

Statewide means nobody can point.

The Alaska Stroke Coalition takes $3,156,626 for an AI imaging network across 21 acute care hospitals, running on existing systems with no new imaging hardware. The state publishes no list of which 21. MapHabit and the Statewide Independent Living Council are statewide too.

A planning year buys a map.

Tanana Chiefs Conference takes $250,000 to plan drone pharmacy from a Fairbanks hub to 42 Interior villages across 94,000 square miles. It is one of 19 planning awards. No aircraft is bought.

The count of eight is a keyword search of the state's own award titles and summaries. It is not a state category. Every dollar here is preliminary and the state says minor adjustments may occur.

The first Friday had none of them.

August 7th moved $4.5 million across 19 projects and not one of the eight was in it. August 21st moved $130 million across 105 projects and five of the eight were. The machines arrived in the middle of the month, not at the start.

Two drones released 374.3 grams of silver iodide over the Kenai Peninsula on August 23rd, about the mass of a can of soup.

Nineteen flares burned over the Kenai. Alaska got one number.

Two drones. Seven missions. Nineteen flares.

Rainmaker says drones EL-151 and EL-153 released 19 silver iodide flares over the Kenai on August 23rd, between 06:38, 18 and 09:33, 41 UTC. Missions 4 through 7 were flown by EL-151 alone.

374.3 grams of silver iodide, over a modelled 249.53 square kilometres.

Each flare dispersed about 19.7 grams over a nominal 3.5 minute burn. The company puts the wet area at 249.53 square kilometres, about 0.6 percent of the borough's land.

Silver iodide only works between minus 5 and minus 15.

Every median release temperature landed inside that window. Soundings launched from the site put the average freezing level at 1,874 metres, and that sounding is the night's one direct measurement.

A low in the Gulf. Northeasterly flow. Nobody watching.

The radar looks from 1,800 metres up.

The company says its range does not cover what happens to precipitation between the lowest radar beam and the ground.

Every retelling was narrower than the one before.

The report says estimates.

A gap in the record is not a finding.

Six things were checked. Three came back.

items.content_html:
73 percent of Alaska likely voters back pausing new data centers until the state passes a law. Houston in the Mat-Su voted a ban down.

73 PERCENT SAID PAUSE.

The one council that voted said no.

The ban lost

An ordinance to block data center construction inside Houston city limits failed on a 4 to 2 vote. The same night the council unanimously approved two resolutions objecting to the state's land transfer process.

73 percent said pause. 63 percent of Republicans agreed.

The poll reached 605 likely voters by text message and web panel, in English, weighted to look like the electorate. The margin is plus or minus 4 points on the whole sample.

One flew the storm. One flew ahead of it.

It reads three things, then it asks.

items.title: A Plan, a Study, and No Published Due Date
items.summary: The agenda with every result row blank, both senators in their own words, and the record as sheets stamped READ or 403.
items.content_html:
At 10:00 a.m. on August 5th, a Senate committee in room SR-253 took up five bills. Three carry AI or a chatbot in the title.

The first federal answer to talking toys is a plan and a study.

Two agencies owe a plan. One academy owes a study.

Per Senator Duckworth's release, the Federal Trade Commission and the Consumer Product Safety Commission must give Congress what the release calls a "coordinated, actionable plan" on AI-enabled toy products. The National Academies must run a comprehensive study.

The due date is not on the record.

The text of S. 5171 returned a 403 on August 15th, so no deadline for the plan or for the study could be read. The committee's own meeting page carries the agenda and no tally for any of the five bills.

Five bills that morning. Three of them AI.

The committee met at 10:00 a.m. on August 5th in room SR-253, entering through SR-254. Three Coast Guard nomination lists were on the same agenda. Senator Duckworth's office announced that day that S. 5171 passed.

Knives, pills and matches.

"discussing sexually explicit content and explaining where to find knives, pills and matches in the home"

The Alaskan on the bill is buying knowledge.

Murkowski is the Republican cosponsor named in the announcement. Read fairly, the bill buys knowledge and writes no rule, which is the normal opening move for a technology nobody has measured yet. Whether that is enough is the argument.

A plan is not a rule. A study is not a standard.

Alaska's own record, as one column tells it.

House Bill 47 provisions criminalizing AI-generated child sexual abuse material and deepfake harassment became law in June.

Five places the record was asked. One answered.

Save this for the next time a talking toy shows up in your house.

items.title: The Equal-Award Projection, 552 to 1
items.summary: The rule in NSF's own words, the $100 million headline against the solicitation's range, and fifty states drawn at true land area.
items.content_html:
Alaska is 570,641 square miles of land, about 552 times Rhode Island's 1,034.

One award per state. Alaska is 552 Rhode Islands.

BY LAND AREA. U.S. CENSUS BUREAU. C23 C24

Fifty states. Fifty identical marks.

Every state is drawn at its true relative area through one projection. Every mark is the same size, because the rule is the same size. NSF anticipates ten awards per cycle.

Only one award per state or multi-state region will be made.

An institution may appear as a participant in at most one proposal.

Ten awards. One cycle.

NSF announced the program as a $100 million initiative. The solicitation puts anticipated funding at $40 million to $100 million. It expects a proposal to request $4 million to $12 million over five years.

Today, access to this infrastructure is highly uneven across the nation.

570,641

Alaska's land area. The largest of any state. About 552 times Rhode Island's 1,034 square miles.

Spreading it is the point.

Spreading a national program across the whole country is a defensible thing to want, and it is the reason the cap exists. It also makes the largest state and the smallest one the same unit of need.

82 days to the deadline.

Subsequent deadlines fall on the first Wednesday in November. A state that misses this cycle is not shut out, it waits a year. That is the difference between a ceiling and a cliff.

Save this. The deadline is November 4th.
